items.title:
In my long read on the Kimi K3 situation, I focus on the big picture for where we going next.

0. Ch...
items.content:
In my long read on the Kimi K3 situation, I focus on the big picture for where we going next.

0. Chinese labs have 3 of top 8 most intelligent models, and have been climbing the ranking.

1. China’s recommits to open-source AI – showing a different (lower) read on near-term risks

2. Open models as the economic Achilles heel of frontier labs (as @deanwball said), and why this can be good for the ecosystem

3. China’s efficiency advantage is letting them make the best models for less, pointing to them staying competitive 

4. A growing ecosystem of frontier, open models is coming soon

5. We are at the very beginning of a long story of frontier open-weight policy, which is extremely complex and something we are not handling well

Kimi K3 is really the beginning, or the reset, of all these stories. I expect to continue to unpack them regularly.

This is incredible. I’ve already posted a few of my thoughts about this result, so I won’t repeat myself. I just wanted to point out a few things:

1. As of this reposting, the original tweet has garnered 10M views. For a nerdy post in pure math, that’s insane. 

2. This result announcement is yet another example of how AI-driven research results are being reported - on Twitter, with no carefully written long article in highly gatekept publications, such as journals, arxiv, and other such BS.

This is how scientific communications were originally conducted. I am so excited that we are going back to that model.

items.title:
Like good odds I'm wrong but I wanted to write this down:

It's pretty clear to me that superintelli...
items.content:
Like good odds I'm wrong but I wanted to write this down:

It's pretty clear to me that superintelligence is here and it's more powerful than us and it's moving where things are going now, not humans anymore

I don't see many people realize this yet, it feels like that pic I posted the other day, everyone is running after the same carrot which is the AI, thinking they're special, and their work is special and their use of AI is special, but it's really not, we're all mostly making the same slop, I mean it's nice slop, useful slop but everyone is making the same slop

And because it's so fast to make things, like people used to spend a year on just building an app, now it's done in hours, it's such an immense change, people send me their projects and it all looks the same, it's useful but it's slop

Non-technical people (e.g. the gfs) are now building the same or better things than technical people like us

So AI has made everybody is just as capable as everyone else, it equalized everyone in the world, as in everyone can make everything (software, music, images, art etc) now and everyone is equal, at least in the digital realm now

And maybe now we're in some odd transitionary time where we have to find out waht the next differentiator is as coding/building/execution isn't one anymore for sure

I thought it'd be distribution but who knows, obviously creativity and ideas, but if you can copy a successful apps in an hour, then how does that differentiating work? 

A guy on here @aporia9n wrote how he increasingly meets founders who blast through apps/products/startups, kind of money grabs, very quickly jumping on a trend, building super quickly with AI, make lots of money quick, everyone copies them, then their margins go to 0%, and they shut it down and go to the next thing, in a way they found one differentiator which is speed

That's one way to do it, but it shows how radically things are changing I think

For now I think the only ones winning is the AI superintelligence itself and the companies providing the AI

> Last week I got to look through 80+ applications from a seed-level incubator batch, through a friend
> Every website was a 8/10, all vaguely similar, and the copy and grammar were a solid 8/10. All were "in principle fundable," because even the TAM analyses, the metric projections, and most importantly the MVPs were "equally decent."
> Honestly, in some cases the differentiating element was very hard to find.

This is exactly my experience, almost everyone around me thinks they're being extremely productive but everyone making the same slop tools, sites, apps etc.

I mean I know I am

Everyone has fixed the low hanging fruit, like I fixed all my server set up, I built a situation monitor that tracks everything like my Ubuntu version, PHP version, updates, it checks the freshness of my backups

Everything works really well now, thanks to AI

But did I or anyone I know make anything really groundbreaking? It's all great but kinda average? Like how image gen of AI is always kinda average? I'm pro-AI of course but I'm just telling you what I think, it's all kinda bland?

I also haven't seen anyone make anything that actually increased revenue for them, lots of internal tools and automation that makes everyone's lives easier for sure, like less/no support, automatic fixes of bugs, great great, but where's the groundbreaking stuff?

But maybe that comes next year? I have no clue

items.title:
Also some thing I forgot to add

There's so many things now where I don't even use the app anymore b...
items.content:
Also some thing I forgot to add

There's so many things now where I don't even use the app anymore but just generate my own app to do things

Like WHOOP, for years I wanted to know the correlation between stuff I do and my workouts and sleep, like going to sauna, or what I eat. WHOOP has a journal but it's practically unusable, I logged sauna for ahwile, then I realized you have to ALSO log the days you DO NOT go to sauna, by hand, every day! Useless

So in those cases I just ask Claude Code to build a little web app for me that pulls all my data in from my WHOOP, and what I eat, my @wip logs when I go to sauna, or go tan, or go gym etc. It just pulls all the data in and gives me the answers to questions I have

Half the time I don't even use the web app it generates, I just ask it directly stuff

I have to find a hotel now for some trips we go, I didn't even go to my own site Hotelist, I just asked Claude Code on my Hotelist VPS server to find me a hotel, etc.

So many times where it just saves more time to ask Claude Code directly stuff than try to do it with some startup/company's app

That's what I mean, I'm obviously more tech than regular people, but we usually slightly ahead in how we use tools, and if I stop using websites and apps, and just use Claude Code for everything in my life, it's not without logic to think that something like that will be the future for most people

And of course it's already happening with Claude Cowork and Codex app which regular non-tech people use

My point is that the entire app and website layer is just getting decimated

And me being a person who lived kinda in that layer (well more websites ofc to be honest) means I have no clue where it's going to except this, or what a person should do, for the first time, I have no clue

The only thing I know is that the superintelligence clanker can't reach into IRL and hardware yet for the next few years at least, and there's lots of stuff there to do that's differentiating, because you need a space, tools, machines, make things, and no you can't generate that in 3 minutes with an AI

Blood, sweat and tears are not automated yet by AI, yet!!!!

Given that even the open-weight models are now close to 3T parameters and Fable is rumored to have 6-8T parameters, by the end of the year we might see models with 20T parameters and larger.

Being able to run the inference of such colossal models might be the only remaining moat.

By the way, the training corpora are also measured in tens of trillions of tokens, so we will have roughly one floating-point number per token, which should be sufficient to absorb the corpus without loss.

Thinking Machines just shipped a 975B model that runs like 41B.

Their open-weights model is called ...
items.content:
Thinking Machines just shipped a 975B model that runs like 41B.

Their open-weights model is called Inkling. Most of its parameters stay idle during inference.

Context stretches to one million tokens. The license is Apache 2.0.

> Top U.S. open-weights score
> 25,000 output tokens average
> Elo 1238 on agent work
> $1.00 in, $4.05 out

It scored 41 on Artificial Analysis. That leads every other U.S. open-weights entry on the board.

You can raise thinking effort for hard coding. You can drop it for volume tasks.

NVFP4 quantization cuts self-host memory. VRAM falls from about 2 TB to roughly 600 GB.

Day-0 serving is live on major routers. We map the sparse routing and the price path.

We also show when closed APIs still win the edge cases.

You don't need an agent for everything.

Good engineering principles still apply. Simplicity still wins.

We need common sense back.

🆕In the Land of AI Agents, the Verifiers Are King

https://t.co/XAesWQUMEn

@tariqshaukat, CEO of @SonarSource, takes to the keynote stage to answer @trq212's challenge of extracting AI utility from slop! Backed by CMU and Sonar productivity studies, he proposes a 3-stage framework

- Stage 1: Guide (Providing context and constraints)
- Stage 2: Verify (Zero-trust, multi-layered verification)
- Stage 3: Solve (Maintenance loops and technical debt control)

Echoing @headinthebox and @varun_pant_'s talks - he is keen on systems thinking and code verification as the key to success with AI. When done right, they have been seeing as much as 92% reduction in issues with disciplined verification with an agent centric development cycle (yes, the ACDC). Closing the full loop is not just needed for the software factory, but for AI Engineering to progress from tokenmaxxing to provably useful code.

items.title: This is awesome. Instead of doing work this morning, I spent some time brushing up on math to provid...
items.content:
This is awesome. Instead of doing work this morning, I spent some time brushing up on math to provide a handwavy overview to anyone else who like me doesn't have a math background and is rusty: 

At a distance, the conjecture is basically that if a n-dimensional polynomial function (e.g. F(x, y, z) map to some output (x', y', z')) meets some special conditions, then 1) it is invertible, and 2) the inverse is polynomial. 

Disproving the conjecture requires finding a n-dimensional polynomial function that meets these special conditions, but is either 1) not invertible at all, or 2) is invertible but not polynomial. (2) is actually not a possibility due to some other math theorem - if there is an inverse, the inverse has to be polynomial. 

Invertibility just means the function can be "undone" at every single input point - if input (x1, y1, z1) maps to output (x2, y2, z2), then output (x2, y2, z2) can map to input (x1, y1, z1). A function is not invertible if multiple input points (x, y, z)'s map to the same output (x, y, z)

Here Fable 5 presumably did some search and found a function that was not invertible. 

That function is this:  
F(x, y, z) = (
z(1+xy)^3 + y^2(1+xy)(4+3xy),
y+3x(1+xy)^2z + 3xy^2(4+3xy),
2x-3x^2y-x^3z
)

This function meets the special conditions (jacobian determinant is a non-zero constant for every point), but has multiple input points that map to the same output: 

Inputs: (0, 0, -1/4), (1, -3/2, 13/2), and (-1, 3/2, 13/2)
all map to the same output: (-1/4, 0, 0)

-----

The Jacobian is the multivariable version of a derivative, so it is a function of a specific input point. When the Jacobian determinant is non-zero at a specific input point, there is local invertibility around that point. This conjecture was stronger in that if it was non-zero (and constant, due to being over the complex numbers, which I don't quite get and I ran out of time to understand), then the function is globally invertible. 

-----

What's interesting here is that finding counterexamples seem like the type of math work that agentic models excel at. It involves generating and crawling a large search space, using priors to narrow it down, and a bit of brute force and raw compute power. Machines can process a wide set of possibilities faster than humans, which is helpful for finding counterexamples.

items.title: This endurance cyclist is preparing to attempt what no one has done: ride solo and unsupported acros...
items.content:
This endurance cyclist is preparing to attempt what no one has done: ride solo and unsupported across Antarctica to the South Pole.

The expedition, slated for this November, means roughly two months alone on the ice, hauling a sled of supplies through temperatures below minus 40 and wind speeds that can top 200 km/h.

And James Benson-King has been using ChatGPT as his only trainer.

Rather than assembling a team of specialist coaches for endurance, strength, and cold-weather survival, Benson-King built his own program with ChatGPT, blending every discipline into one adjustable system.

He’s leaned on it in the field too, troubleshooting a broken stove in the Icelandic highlands and designing workouts around whatever gear he had on hand already.

Benson-King thinks the approach compressed three years of prep into one. He’s no novice, either: he holds a Guinness World Record and once cycled Alaska to Argentina.

items.title:
Serveless, but for models, is here!

I stopped renting servers 12 years ago. I mostly moved everythi...
items.content:
Serveless, but for models, is here!

I stopped renting servers 12 years ago. I mostly moved everything to serverless functions.

It's taken a long time for this idea to work with AI models.

The issue was simple: You can start a simple function in milliseconds and scale it down to zero for free, but loading a 20GB model into memory takes quite a bit of time.

And once the model was loaded, forget about shutting it down. You'd better pay for an idle GPU than force the next user to wait while everything reloads.

So you have two options:

1. Optimize for low-latency answers and pay for an idle GPU, or
2. Optimize for lower costs by scaling to zero and making users wait

Both are bad, and fortunately, we don't need to choose anymore.

Runpod, the new AI developer cloud, is doing something really clever to solve this problem:

• They don't shut down idle models
• Instead, they move them to somewhere cheaper
• When traffic returns, they page the model back to the GPU

This whole process is extremely fast: cold starts drop below 200ms for busy endpoints. They call this technique "FlashBoot".

On top of that, to deploy your models, they ditched Docker because they don't want you spending time rebuilding a massive image every time you change a line. Instead, you get a Python function with a line for the GPU you need. You can deploy in seconds with this.

The first run is always the slowest because you're installing dependencies, but after that, you can run very large models very quickly.

In summary:

1. Serverless is here for models
2. You don't need a better GPU
3. It's actually 90% cheaper than 90% of what big clouds give you

items.title: I’ve decided to put a major theoretical algorithmic project I’ve been using AI to work on on a back-...
items.content: I’ve decided to put a major theoretical algorithmic project I’ve been using AI to work on on a back-burner. Even though there has been some good progress on it, including a proved lower bound, the upper bound remains extremely difficult and elusive. Proving or disproving it would probably require development of a whole new machinery from scratch, and far more time and compute than I had anticipated. I’ll still let have GPT 5.6 work on it intermittently, but it looks like the best option right now would be to wait for GPT 6 to drop. Hopefully we are still allowed to have it.

items.title:
A career plan that waits for stability is already late.

Digital work keeps changing through new too...
items.content:
A career plan that waits for stability is already late.

Digital work keeps changing through new tools and expectations, so people need learning close to daily tasks and judgment where automation stops before roles drift away from them. 

Microblog  by  @antgrasso  #FutureOfWork

Career resilience is built inside daily work, not outside it.

Learning has to stay close to real tasks, because new tools only matter when they improve decisions and help people work with more confidence.

Adaptability also needs direction.

Changing with every new platform can create noise, while a clear professional identity helps people understand which skills to grow and which habits to leave behind.

Experience still matters, but it has to be converted into future readiness.

Feedback helps when it reveals useful patterns; professional networks help when they give people better context for change.

Digital presence is part of this process.

Credibility online comes from useful contributions and consistent communication, while trust grows through time rather than visibility alone. 

The practical lesson is simple: careers need maintenance like any living system.

Skills and judgment should be updated before change forces the update.

items.title:
People are wasting their AI subscriptions.

They don’t realize how powerful AI can be in achieving t...
items.content:
People are wasting their AI subscriptions.

They don’t realize how powerful AI can be in achieving their own goals. 

They’re asking AI to reply to emails with zero goals in mind and nothing laddering up to “the big picture”. 

I was that kid where if my parents asked me to clean my room, I wouldn’t do it. 

They could tell me royalty was coming over, and I still wouldn’t do it. 

But if they said, “Bet you can’t clean your room in the next 5 minutes!”, that place would be spotless. 

When things are gamified and it becomes a personal challenge against myself, I am bought IN. 

I use that trick with AI today. 

Anything that feels tedious but really gets me closer to achieving my goals, I just make Claude build me a gaming interface to get it done. 

Oh you have to provide feedback on roundtable interview questions? Great. The interface is gray with canons and arrows as decoration. A knight is in the background, riding toward a castle to save his horse’s best donkey friend. Every question you fix and/or approve, the knight gets closer to the donkey. If you finish in under 6 minutes, the donkey is saved. And if you complete it this week instead of next week, he can save 100 donkeys. 

Hack your brain with AI. 

Consider the actual way you’ve been motivated in the past (yes, even if it’s insane to admit) and ask Claude/Codex to reorient its own work toward that motivation style.

items.title: Yesterday I was fortunate enough to go to my first-ever World Cup game, with my long-time colleagues...
items.content:
Yesterday I was fortunate enough to go to my first-ever World Cup game, with my long-time colleagues/friends @OriolVinyalsML and @quocleix and their spouses).  We were sitting in the corner area and had a quite good view of the goal!

I present to you a 43 second multi-part drama filled with emotion:

The initial promising-looking cross coming in, but looking overhit

Nico Williams cleverly knocking it down at the back post into a dangerous area

Ferran Torres striking it cleanly into the roof of the net

The crowd rising as one (forcing me to stand up as well)

The elation of the Spanish players racing off the bench to celebrate

The dejection of the Argentinian players, their defense having finally been breached in extra time

The elation of my Spanish colleague Oriol and his wife Meire next to me (he and I are both Barça fans, so it was nice to see a Barça player score the winning goal)

The entire stadium reacting

Whew!

2. These agents can code and run continuously
3. You can use specialized "departments" from a marketplace

Thanks to the Matrix team for partnering with me on this post.

He is one of USA’s highest national security officers.

I would t...
items.content:
I just saw @BalaSelvam follow me.

He is one of USA’s highest national security officers.

I would tell him to visit @reservoirfarms.

The farmers are America’s secret asset.

Automate them and save the family farm.

Why do we call it the homeland?

Because without them we are starving.

They have interesting ideas about how to sense whether their robot will get stuck in the mud ahead or not. You don’t want your robots stuck in the mud, do you?

I know a guy who built a robot on a potato farm in Idaho.

Built key parts of Niantic’s augmented reality system.

And if I were talking to Trump I would be trying to convince him to support robots.

Which include drones. 

With an economic zone with big economic incentives.

But this isn’t his favorite territory so I have a big jump to get over.

Glad I don’t have your job but thankful someone is doing it.

Here's the scenario no one wants to admit is their reality:

→ Sensor detects an anomaly on the fact...
items.content:
Here's the scenario no one wants to admit is their reality:

→ Sensor detects an anomaly on the factory floor
→ Data travels to the cloud
→ Cloud processes it
→ Decision comes back

Meanwhile? The machines kept moving.

In industrial environments, that round trip can create operational risks.

Milliseconds matter when you're monitoring pressure, temperature, robotic systems, and safety thresholds simultaneously.

Speed in these settings isn't a nice-to-have.

It can be critical for safety-sensitive operations.

Move the intelligence closer to the operation.

The intelligence runs where the data is created.

→ Starlink connectivity
→ Integrated connectivity designed to support resilient operations

Because connected systems increasingly rely on resilient network infrastructure.

items.title:
Grape vines would rather be cut by human hands than machine ones. 

Sarah Francis Ackerman, showed m...
items.content:
Grape vines would rather be cut by human hands than machine ones. 

Sarah Francis Ackerman, showed me the results of a blind A/B test that showed that to be true. Had two barrels of the same wine, one cut by hand. One cut by machine.

Her wine was the first female made wine to get a perfect score from Robert Parker. 

One thing I don’t talk about often is that her winery was destroyed in the Napa Earthquake. It broke all her glassware. She couldn’t operate without $100,000 to replace all that.

I invited her to give everyone a taste at my 51st party and tell her story. Had a couple of hundred who showed up because my wife and I try to curate fun times. Several invested which saved her winery. I was bawling when she was talking.

How did I meet her? My wife and I had a Tesla Tour. A local business drives people around the valley and gives you an insider look at Napa.

That took us to a winery where she introduced us to her winery.

Turns out she is one of the best story tellers I have ever met.

And I mean that in the good way. She grew up talking to her parents vines as a child. They were as close as her family, she told me.

Many farmers have stories of getting close to their crops. But hers comes with a Southern Charm that is quite endearing and memorable.

She took me into Napa’s best vineyard where she had a row of grapes (the vineyard she was in is on her label). While walking me through the vines she casually drops that she usually sleeps out in the vineyard with the grapes.

Which saved another winery because she saw a disease spreading long before it would have been discovered by them.

Can we make a robot that fools the plant into thinking it is being cut by human hands?

Yes. Which makes it economically feasible to do.

So if you block robots you are blocking better wine.

Everything will be affected by AI. Some in different ways than others.

items.summary_html: Argues that openly sharing expertise, like bloggers did, generally attracts more business despite fears of giving away value.
items.content_html:
@rookepoole Bloggers went through the same argument. The argument was: if we give away everything about who we are—like if you're a plumber writing a blog about how to change a shower—we'll lose business.

The thing is, everybody who did share, and shared openly, actually got a lot of business. Maybe people don't need you for that specific fix, but they will need you for something else, and you've proven you have the expertise.

It usually works out like that, though some people do get screwed. It's life, man.

items.content:
@BlissAICyber True!

Plus, she talked to us about how she convinced Beckstoffer to give her a row of grapes in his most expensive vineyard. By the way, the best wine Napa's ever made was actually three rows from her grapes, so it's a pretty good vineyard (high quality for making Cabernet). Many say it's the best in the world.

She made wine in Alabama, if I remember right, which is a really tough place to make wine. She got noticed because of that, but she told us she met the owner of this vineyard and convinced him that she would do a better job with his vines than anybody else in Napa Valley. 

It goes back to sleeping with the vines when she was a child, because that gave her the storytelling ability to convince someone like him to give her his most expensive vines.

items.title: @UID_ @wol Ik zat eind Mei in Voco in Den Haag waar de AC nauwelijks werkte, was begrensd op 23'C wa...
items.content:
@UID_ @wol Ik zat eind Mei in Voco in Den Haag waar de AC nauwelijks werkte, was begrensd op 23'C wat realistisch leidde tot 25'C in de kamer, de ramen zaten op slot ("due to security reasons" zei de Amerikaanse frontdeskdame)

Ik ben niet het persoon om te liegen hierover, ik reis veel rond en ook in Europa, en geen enkele plek in de wereld waar telkens de AC begrensd is, nauwelijks of niets werkt

Budget is ook niet het probleem, ik zit in hotels van €100 to €1500 ze hebben vaak allemaal hetzelfde probleem, de duurde hotels vaak nog meer omdat ze zich meer willen profileren als klimaatbewust etc.

Ik train 3x per week gewichten, 3x per week cardio, voor mijn gezondheid, en ben dus gezond en redelijk fit (meeste mensen hebben overgewicht zoals je weet) en dan is 18C slapen de beste temperatuur, dat zegt ook de wetenschap. Als je heel dik of dun bent of ongezond bent, ben je vaak koud dus dan is 24C slapen prima

Je ziet dat West Europeanen in het algemeen meer cardio doen (rennen, fietsen etc) dan krachttraining, dus dat leidt tot een ander soort lichaam, minder spiermassa dan heb je het kouder

Je gaat natuurlijk zeggen, wat lult die mongool, maar ik vertel gewoon uit mijn eigen ervaring

Mijn ideaal is dat je in Europa zelf mag kiezen welke temperatuur je slaapt, en dat ze het niet begrenzen. Ik vind het zelf niet logisch om AC te beperken, beter dat iedereen zijn ideale temperatuur vindt en daarop kan slapen en werken

Te hete temperaturen om te werken is ook niet goed, en dan kunnen mensen niet goed meer denken, en dat leidt uiteindelijk tot minder innovatie, en dan minder rijkdom

Singapore is een goed voorbeeld, de vader des vaderlands Lee Kuan Yew zei dat AC een van de redenen was dat Singapore rijk kon worden in de hete vochtige jungle dicht bij de evenaar!
